caption:
The European Commission confirmed it was hit by a cyberattack carried out with AI tools.
Payroll, leave and medical claim systems went offline for days.
No staff wide data breach has been found so far.

Should AI hacking tools be public at all?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

threads_text: Hackers used AI tools to hit the European Commission, and staff payroll and leave systems went offline for days. It is the first AI cyberattack the EU has ever reported. Should AI hacking tools be allowed in public?

site_article.headline: European Commission confirms cyberattack carried out with AI tools
site_article.dek: Staff payroll, leave and medical reimbursement systems were taken offline after an attack first detected on October 22.
site_article.summary: The European Commission confirmed that an attack detected on October 22, 2026, was carried out with AI tools. Internal HR systems were disrupted for at least 10 days, according to Politico.
site_article.seo_description: The European Commission says hackers used AI tools in an attack found Oct. 22 that took payroll, leave and medical claim systems offline for at least 10 days.
site_article.answer_summary: The European Commission confirmed it was hit by an AI-assisted cyberattack, first detected on October 22, 2026, that disrupted internal staff systems. It says no staff wide data breach has been found.
site_article.hero_alt: European Union flags flying outside EU headquarters in Brussels.

paragraphs.text: The European Commission confirmed on Thursday, November 19, 2026, that it had been hit by a cyberattack carried out with the help of AI tools. Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the first signs of the attack were detected on October 22 and that an investigation was opened, according to The Record and the Associated Press.

The AP reported that it was the first time the 27 member European Union had reported a cyberattack using an AI tool. Regnier said AI assisted tools can be used, and misused, to find weaknesses in systems, and confirmed that the attack was done with AI tools.
Payroll, leave and medical claims went offline

Politico first reported the attack and said it disrupted internal services for at least 10 days. According to The Register, the Commission took offline Sysper, the system staff use for payslips, timesheets and vacation requests, and MyPMO, which handles medical reimbursements. Translation services were also affected.

The Register reported that both systems came back online earlier in the week, but that Sysper went down again on Wednesday, November 18. Some staff could not book leave or submit timesheets, while salaries were paid as usual, according to Politico's reporting cited by The Register.

Regnier said several applications were taken down temporarily as a protective measure and that most have since been restored. He said the Commission had found no evidence of a data breach affecting its staff as a whole, and The Record reported that there was no known ransom demand.

Politico's sources said the EU's cybersecurity team, CERT-EU, identified ARTEX, a publicly available AI powered penetration testing framework. CERT-EU published a warning about ARTEX in early November, and The Record reported that the FBI had warned a week earlier that criminals and state sponsored groups were using it.

The Register reported that the developer of ARTEX removed its GitHub repository in October, but copies were already circulating. The Commission did not name the tool, the attackers or their motive, and Regnier said the investigation was still open.

According to The Brussels Times, the Commission's Corporate Management Board held an urgent meeting in early November, and Executive Vice President Henna Virkkunen briefed other commissioners on Wednesday. Regnier rejected suggestions that the incident had been kept quiet, saying that publicizing defenses could weaken them.

The case shows how penetration testing tools built for defenders can be turned around by attackers once they are public, and how an attack on back office systems such as payroll and leave requests can disrupt a large institution for weeks without a confirmed data theft.

Watch for the results of the Commission's investigation, including whether staff personal data was viewed and whether any group is named, and for further warnings from CERT-EU and the FBI about ARTEX.
